vignette:
She is 69 and still goes to work most mornings, tying on the fast-food apron with the same careful movements she has used for years, though her body now seems to brace before her mind does. She is a Middle Eastern woman, married, and she speaks about her family with a kind of steady pride, as if they are the central frame of her life. Until the stalking began, she describes herself as independent, practical, and someone who could handle hardship. She had worked long hours, kept her home, and moved through her neighborhood without much concern. That sense of ordinary safety changes when a man she knows only slightly begins appearing where she is.

At first, the contact feels unsettling but easy to explain away. He notices her in places she visits regularly and starts making comments that feel too familiar, too personal. She tries to be polite, then distant, then direct. Instead of stopping, he becomes more persistent. He waits near her route, shows up around her workplace, and leaves her feeling watched even when she cannot see him. She begins to scan parking lots before getting out of the car. She looks over her shoulder in the grocery store. Her attention narrows to exits, windows, mirrors, and reflections. She describes the first period as a kind of confusion mixed with shame-she keeps asking herself whether she is misunderstanding his behavior, whether she has somehow invited it, whether she is overreacting. That self-doubt makes it harder to tell others how afraid she is.

As the stalking continues, her fear becomes organized around daily life. She changes the times she leaves home. She varies her route to work. She asks her husband to walk her to the car and begins relying on him more than she likes to admit. At work, where she takes orders and cleans tables at a pace that leaves little room for reflection, she still feels the pressure of his presence. The dining room noise, the smell of fries, the rhythm of customers coming and going should be familiar and grounding, but instead she finds herself watching the door each time it opens. She startles easily when someone stands too close behind her. Her hands tremble when she carries drinks. She keeps her voice controlled and professional, but inside she is often counting seconds until the shift ends.

At home, the fear follows her. She checks locks repeatedly and sometimes circles the house before going to bed, needing to look at the windows one more time. She has difficulty sleeping because once the lights are off her mind fills with possibilities: him outside, him calling, him finding a way in. When she does sleep, it is light and broken by dreams that leave her shaken. She wakes with her heart racing and then lies awake, listening. She says the worst part is not only what he might do, but not knowing when he will appear again. That uncertainty keeps her constantly on guard, as if her body has forgotten how to stand down.

Her relationships narrow as the stalking persists. She becomes less social and declines invitations she once would have enjoyed. She does not want to burden her children, and she feels embarrassed that this is happening at her age, as if she should be beyond being frightened in this way. She is tense and irritable with her husband at times, especially when he urges her not to dwell on it. She knows he means well, but she experiences his reassurance as distance from the danger she feels so clearly. She has moments of anger toward herself for being unable to think of anything else, followed by sadness when she realizes how much of her energy goes into trying to feel safe.

Over time, she notices that she is not quite the same person inside her own life. She is more easily startled by unexpected sounds, more suspicious of unfamiliar cars, more exhausted by the effort of staying alert. Even when nothing is happening, she feels as though something might. She still shows up for work, still cares for her family, still moves through her routines, but she does so with an undercurrent of dread that shapes the day. When she speaks about the stalking now, there is a heaviness in her voice, as if she has been carrying the experience for so long that it has become part of her posture, her sleep, and the way she looks into every room before she settles down.
